drug_class: Anti-VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitor) / biosimilar ophthalmic agent
purpose: Ranibizumab-nuna is used to treat certain eye conditions that can cause vision loss, including wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), diabetic macular edema, and abnormal blood vessel growth in the eye. It helps protect your vision and in some cases may even improve it. Your eye doctor will determine if this medication is right for your specific condition.
how_it_works: In some eye diseases, the body makes too much of a protein called VEGF, which causes leaky or abnormal blood vessels to grow in the eye. These abnormal vessels can damage your vision. Ranibizumab-nuna works by blocking that protein, stopping the growth of those harmful blood vessels and reducing fluid leakage in the eye. Think of it like a plug that stops the problem from getting worse.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include eye redness, eye pain or discomfort, small floaters or spots in your vision, increased eye pressure, and a feeling that something is in your eye. Some patients may also notice temporary blurry vision right after the injection. Most of these effects are mild and go away on their own.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have any eye infections or eye inflammation before receiving this medication, as it should not be given during an active infection. There is a small risk of serious eye infection (endophthalmitis) or retinal detachment after the injection. Seek immediate medical attention if you notice sudden vision loss, severe eye pain, increased redness, or sensitivity to light after treatment. Also let your doctor know if you have had a recent stroke or heart attack, as this medication may slightly increase the risk of blood clot-related events.
typical_dosing: This medication is given as an injection directly into the eye by your eye doctor in a clinical setting — you will not give this to yourself at home. The typical dose is 0.5 mg injected once a month, though your doctor may adjust the schedule based on how your eye responds to treatment. Some patients may eventually need fewer injections over time.
